claim: Temozolomide (TMZ) is the primary chemotherapeutic drug used in glioblastoma treatment.
source: Temozolomide (TMZ), a DNA methylating agent, is the primary chemotherapeutic drug used in glioblastoma treatment.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract without supporting data in the manuscript itself, but represents established clinical knowledge.

claim: TMZ induces mostly N-alkylation adducts (N7-methylguanine and N3-methyladenine).
source: TMZ induces mostly N-alkylation adducts (N7-methylguanine and N3-methyladenine) and some O6-methylguanine (O6mG) adducts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation to established literature on alkylating agent chemistry.

claim: TMZ induces some O6-methylguanine (O6mG) adducts.
source: TMZ induces mostly N-alkylation adducts (N7-methylguanine and N3-methyladenine) and some O6-methylguanine (O6mG) adducts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation to established literature on alkylating agent chemistry.

claim: During DNA replication, thymine is incorporated across from O6mG.
source: Current models propose that during DNA replication, thymine is incorporated across from O6mG, promoting a futile cycle of mismatch repair (MMR) that leads to DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs).
evidence: This is stated as part of current models in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Thymine incorporation across from O6mG promotes a futile cycle of mismatch repair (MMR).
source: Current models propose that during DNA replication, thymine is incorporated across from O6mG, promoting a futile cycle of mismatch repair (MMR) that leads to DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs).
evidence: This is stated as part of current models in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Futile cycles of MMR at O6mG:T mispairs lead to DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs).
source: Current models propose that during DNA replication, thymine is incorporated across from O6mG, promoting a futile cycle of mismatch repair (MMR) that leads to DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs).
evidence: This is stated as part of current models in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: MMR proteins are enriched on MNU-treated DNA in Xenopus egg-derived extracts.
source: We have shown that in this system, MMR proteins are enriched on MNU-treated DNA and we observed robust, MMR-dependent, repair synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1B and described in the Results section.

claim: MNU-treated plasmids exhibit robust, MMR-dependent repair synthesis in Xenopus egg-derived extracts.
source: We have shown that in this system, MMR proteins are enriched on MNU-treated DNA and we observed robust, MMR-dependent, repair synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3, including depletion experiments.

claim: MMR initiated at O6mG:C sites is strongly stimulated in cis by repair processing of other lesions, such as N-alkylation adducts.
source: Our evidence also suggests that MMR, initiated at O6mG:C sites, is strongly stimulated in cis by repair processing of other lesions, such as N-alkylation adducts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing threefold stimulation of MMR at single O6mG:C sites when N-alkyl adducts are present.

claim: MNU-treated plasmids display DSBs in extracts.
source: Importantly, MNU-treated plasmids display DSBs in extracts, the frequency of which increases linearly with the square of alkylation dose.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A showing linear plasmid formation.

claim: The frequency of DSBs in MNU-treated plasmids increases linearly with the square of alkylation dose.
source: Importantly, MNU-treated plasmids display DSBs in extracts, the frequency of which increases linearly with the square of alkylation dose.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B demonstrating quadratic dose-response.

claim: DSBs result from two independent repair processes, one involving MMR at O6mG:C sites and the other involving base excision repair acting at a nearby N-alkylation adduct.
source: We suggest that DSBs result from two independent repair processes, one involving MMR at O6mG:C sites and the other involving base excision repair acting at a nearby N-alkylation adduct.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the quadratic dose-response data and the known repair pathways, representing an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: The mechanism of DSB formation from MNU/TMZ is replication-independent.
source: We propose a new, replication-independent mechanism of action of TMZ, which operates in addition to the well-studied cell cycle-dependent mode of action.
evidence: This is supported by the use of Xenopus extracts containing geminin (a replication inhibitor) and the observation of DSBs under these conditions.

claim: MNU produces 70-75% of total alkyl adducts as N7-methylguanine (7mG).
source: Among the DNA adducts produced by methylating agents such as N-methyl-N-nitrosourea (MNU) and temozolomide (TMZ), a clinically used mimic, the most abundant are two N-alkylation adducts, at the N7 position of guanine (7mG: 70–75% of total alkyl adducts) and the N3 position of adenine (3mA: 8–12%).
evidence: This is cited from Beranek, 1990 in the introduction.

claim: MNU produces 8-12% of total alkyl adducts as N3-methyladenine (3mA).
source: Among the DNA adducts produced by methylating agents such as N-methyl-N-nitrosourea (MNU) and temozolomide (TMZ), a clinically used mimic, the most abundant are two N-alkylation adducts, at the N7 position of guanine (7mG: 70–75% of total alkyl adducts) and the N3 position of adenine (3mA: 8–12%).
evidence: This is cited from Beranek, 1990 in the introduction.

claim: MNU produces 8-9% O-alkylation adducts in the form of O6-methylguanine (O6mG).
source: Importantly, both reagents also produce 8–9% O-alkylation adducts in the form of O6-methylguanine (O6mG).
evidence: This is cited from Beranek, 1990 in the introduction.

claim: MMS forms much lower levels of O6mG (<0.3%) compared to MNU.
source: This feature contrasts with another common methylating agent, methyl-methane sulfonate (MMS), which forms a much lower level of O6mG (<0.3%) while producing similarly high proportions of 7mG (81–83%) and 3mA (10–11%) (Beranek, 1990).
evidence: This is cited from Beranek, 1990 in the introduction.

claim: MMS produces 81-83% of total alkyl adducts as 7mG.
source: This feature contrasts with another common methylating agent, methyl-methane sulfonate (MMS), which forms a much lower level of O6mG (<0.3%) while producing similarly high proportions of 7mG (81–83%) and 3mA (10–11%) (Beranek, 1990).
evidence: This is cited from Beranek, 1990 in the introduction.

claim: MMS produces 10-11% of total alkyl adducts as 3mA.
source: This feature contrasts with another common methylating agent, methyl-methane sulfonate (MMS), which forms a much lower level of O6mG (<0.3%) while producing similarly high proportions of 7mG (81–83%) and 3mA (10–11%) (Beranek, 1990).
evidence: This is cited from Beranek, 1990 in the introduction.

claim: N-alkylation adducts (7mG and 3mA) are repaired by base excision repair (BER).
source: The major N-alkylation (N-alkyl) adducts (7mG and 3mA) are repaired by base excision repair (BER), using N-methylpurine DNA glycosylase (MPG), also known as 3-alkyladenine DNA glycosylase (AAG), and alkylpurine DNA N-glycosylase (APNG) (Chakravarti et al., 1991; Lindahl, 1976).
evidence: This is cited from Chakravarti et al., 1991 and Lindahl, 1976.

claim: O6mG can be directly repaired by O6-methylguanine DNA methyl transferase (MGMT).
source: O-alkylation adducts (O6mG, O4mT) can be directly repaired by O6-methylguanine DNA methyl transferase (MGMT), a protein that transfers the methyl group from these adducts to one of its cysteine residues (Demple et al., 1982; Olsson and Lindahl, 1980; Tano et al., 1990).
evidence: This is cited from Demple et al., 1982; Olsson and Lindahl, 1980; Tano et al., 1990.

claim: MGMT transfers the methyl group from O6mG to one of its cysteine residues.
source: O-alkylation adducts (O6mG, O4mT) can be directly repaired by O6-methylguanine DNA methyl transferase (MGMT), a protein that transfers the methyl group from these adducts to one of its cysteine residues (Demple et al., 1982; Olsson and Lindahl, 1980; Tano et al., 1990).
evidence: This is cited from Demple et al., 1982; Olsson and Lindahl, 1980; Tano et al., 1990.

claim: MMS-induced DSBs arise when replication meets BER-induced single-strand breaks (SSBs) in rodent cells.
source: In rodent cells, it was proposed that MMS-induced DSBs arise when replication meets BER-induced single-strand breaks (SSBs) (Ensminger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Ensminger et al., 2014.

claim: O6mG:T lesions are excellent substrates for MMR.
source: Indeed, O6mG:T lesions were found to be excellent substrates for MMR (Duckett et al., 1999; Yoshioka et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Duckett et al., 1999 and Yoshioka et al., 2006.

claim: When synchronized HeLa cells are treated in G1 with MNU, they continue through the first cell cycle almost normally with little effect on DNA synthesis.
source: A seminal paper, published 50 years ago by Plant and Roberts, 1971, noted that when synchronized HeLa cells are treated in G1 with MNU, they continue through the first cell cycle almost normally and with little effect on DNA synthesis.
evidence: This is cited from Plant and Roberts, 1971.

claim: There is a dramatic effect on DNA synthesis in the second cell cycle after MNU exposure in synchronized HeLa cells.
source: On the other hand, there is a dramatic effect on DNA synthesis in the second cell cycle after MNU exposure.
evidence: This is cited from Plant and Roberts, 1971.

claim: All six canonical MMR proteins (MSH2, MSH3, MSH6, MLH1, PMS1, and PMS2) were specifically enriched on MNU plasmids.
source: All six canonical MMR proteins (MSH2, MSH3, MSH6, MLH1, PMS1, and PMS2) were specifically enriched on MNU plasmids.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: RAD18, POLη, EXO1, and two subunits of Pol delta (POLD2 and POLD3) were specifically enriched on MNU plasmids.
source: Other proteins known to participate in MMR, RAD18, POLη, EXO1, and two subunits of Pol delta (POLD2 and POLD3), were also specifically enriched on MNU plasmids.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No MMR proteins were enriched on MMS-treated plasmids.
source: No MMR proteins were enriched on MMS-treated plasmids (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Recruitment of MMR proteins depends on O6mG.
source: As MNU treatment induces 20–30 times more O6mG adducts than MMS, we postulate that recruitment of MMR proteins depends on O6mG.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential enrichment of MMR proteins on MNU vs MMS-treated plasmids and the known difference in O6mG levels.

claim: MNU- and ENU-treated plasmids sustained robust, time-dependent UDS equivalent to 3-4% of the synthesis needed for a full round of replication.
source: Undamaged plasmids exhibited a low level of background DNA synthesis, whereas MNU- and ENU-treated plasmids sustained robust, time-dependent UDS equivalent to 3–4% of the synthesis needed for a full round of replication (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: MMS-treated plasmids exhibited UDS that was just twofold above the background seen in undamaged plasmids.
source: MMS-treated plasmids exhibited UDS that was just twofold above the background seen in undamaged plasmids (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Depletion of MLH1 or PMS2 severely reduced UDS in MNU-treated plasmids.
source: Depletion of MLH1 or PMS2 severely reduced UDS in MNU-treated plasmids, while no reduction was observed in PMS1-depleted extracts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No reduction in UDS was observed in PMS1-depleted extracts.
source: Depletion of MLH1 or PMS2 severely reduced UDS in MNU-treated plasmids, while no reduction was observed in PMS1-depleted extracts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MutLα (composed of MLH1 and PMS2) is involved in canonical mismatch repair.
source: This observation is consistent with the fact that MutLα (composed of MLH1 and PMS2) is involved in canonical mismatch repair whereas MutLβ (composed of MLH1 and PMS1) is not (Jiricny, 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Jiricny, 2006.

claim: MutLβ (composed of MLH1 and PMS1) is not involved in canonical mismatch repair.
source: This observation is consistent with the fact that MutLα (composed of MLH1 and PMS2) is involved in canonical mismatch repair whereas MutLβ (composed of MLH1 and PMS1) is not (Jiricny, 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Jiricny, 2006.

claim: Aphidicolin decreased incorporation by 3.5-fold on average on MNU and ENU plasmids.
source: Aphidicolin (Aph), an inhibitor of B-family DNA polymerases (Baranovskiy et al., 2014), decreased incorporation, on average, by 3.5-fold on MNU and ENU plasmids while it had a more modest effect on MMS-treated plasmids (1.5-fold) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Aphidicolin had a 1.5-fold effect on MMS-treated plasmids.
source: Aphidicolin (Aph), an inhibitor of B-family DNA polymerases (Baranovskiy et al., 2014), decreased incorporation, on average, by 3.5-fold on MNU and ENU plasmids while it had a more modest effect on MMS-treated plasmids (1.5-fold) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The average repair patch per O6mG adduct is approximately 500 nt long.
source: Evidence obtained with G:T and O6mG:T constructs (see below) indicates that, under present experimental conditions, only about ≈30% of O6mG are substrates for MMR, suggesting that, on average, an MMR patch is ≈500 nt long.
evidence: This is calculated from UDS data and the number of O6mG lesions per plasmid.

claim: The average DNA synthesis patch per N-alkyl adduct is approximately 2.6 nt.
source: With ≈17 N-alkyl adducts per plasmid, the average DNA synthesis patch per adduct, in case all N-alkyl lesions are repaired, is ≈2.6 nt, a value consistent with a mixture of long (≈2–8 nt)- and short-patch (1 nt) BER events at N-alkyl adducts.
evidence: This is calculated from UDS data in MMS-treated plasmids.

claim: In MNU-treated plasmids, open circular repair products were threefold more abundant than closed circular products in the absence of aphidicolin.
source: We also note that in MNU-treated plasmids, in the absence of Aph, open circular repair products were threefold more abundant than closed circular products (Figure 2C; 32P image).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MMR repair was complete in only approximately 25% of MNU-treated plasmid molecules.
source: This observation suggests that MMR repair was complete in only ≈25% of plasmid molecules while 75% of molecules contained at least one nick (or a gap).
evidence: This is inferred from the ratio of closed circular to open circular products in Figure 2C.

claim: There was approximately 50% loss of total DNA in the MNU+Aph lane compared to other lanes.
source: Interestingly, there was a ≈50% loss of total DNA in the MNU+Aph lane compared to the other lanes, suggesting massive DNA degradation in NPE due to polymerase inhibition by Aph.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MNU-treated plasmids did not exhibit significant repair synthesis in HSS extract.
source: In HSS extract, MNU-treated plasmids did not exhibit significant repair synthesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), in contrast to the robust repair synthesis seen in NPE (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: When HSS extract was supplemented with purified AAG glycosylase, robust repair synthesis is observed in MNU-treated plasmids.
source: When HSS extract was supplemented with purified AAG glycosylase (150 nM) (NEB, Biolabs), robust repair synthesis is observed in MNU-treated plasmids (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: A single O6mG:C construct (mGC) triggers MMR-mediated repair synthesis.
source: We observed incorporation of radioactivity specifically attributable to the single O6mG:C lesion (compare mGC with GC in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Repair synthesis due to the single O6mG:C lesion is strongly enhanced by the presence of MMS adducts.
source: Importantly, repair synthesis, due to the single O6mG:C lesion, is strongly enhanced by the presence of MMS adducts (compare mGC+MMS with GC+MMS in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Incorporation due to a single O6mG lesion is stimulated about 2.9-fold by the presence of MMS adducts.
source: One can thus estimate that, incorporation due to a single O6mG lesion, is stimulated about 2.9-fold (1.85/0.64) by the presence in cis of MMS adducts (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is calculated from UDS data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: GT-containing constructs trigger a much stronger MMR response than their GC counterparts.
source: The main observation is that GT-containing constructs trigger a much stronger MMR response than their GC counterparts (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the absence of MMS, the level of UDS in mGC represents 23% of the level in mGT.
source: In the absence of MMS, at the 120′ time point, the level of UDS in mGC represents 23% of the level in mGT.
evidence: This is calculated from UDS data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the presence of MMS, the level of UDS in mGC+MMS represents 38% of the level in mGT+MMS.
source: In the presence of MMS, at the 120′ time point, the level of UDS in mGC+MMS represents 38% of the level in mGT+MMS.
evidence: This is calculated from UDS data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The extent of mGC repair is in the range of 30% compared to mGT repair.
source: In conclusion, supposing that 100% of mGT mispairs are fully repaired, the extent of mGC repair would be in the range of 30%.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of UDS levels between mGC and mGT constructs.

claim: O6mGC-induced repair essentially takes place within the S fragment, with only modest spill-over into the L fragment (10-15%).
source: These results clearly show that O6mGC-induced repair essentially takes place within the S fragment, with only modest spill-over into the L fragment (10–15%).
evidence: This is supported by restriction enzyme analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and 1D.

claim: MMS adducts do not modify the repair pattern but increase the frequency of repair centered at O6mG sites.
source: Thus, MMS adducts do not modify the repair pattern, that is, the relative distribution of 32P incorporation in S and L fragments, but they increase the frequency of repair centered at O6mG sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the restriction enzyme analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: For a twofold increase in MNU exposure, the linear plasmid band increased approximately fourfold.
source: For a twofold increase in MNU exposure, the linear plasmid band increased approximately fourfold (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The quadratic dose-response strongly suggests that DSBs occur as a consequence of two independent repair events at neighboring lesions.
source: This quadratic dose-response strongly suggests that DSBs occur as a consequence of two independent repair events at neighboring lesions, for example a BER event at an N-alkyl adduct leading to a nick in one strand that is encountered by a gap formed by an MMR event initiated at an O6mG site in the opposite strand (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference based on the quadratic dose-response data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the MNU++ sample, no linear ssDNA was left, all the DNA molecules running as a smear centered around the 3000 nt position.
source: In the MNU++ sample, no linear ssDNA was left, all the DNA molecules running as a smear centered around the 3000 nt position (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The double-stranded DNA running as open circular plasmid molecules contain each, on average, three to four nicks per plasmid strand.
source: The observed smear reveals that the double-stranded DNA running as open circular plasmid molecules in the neutral loading gel (Figure 4A) contain each, on average, three to four nicks per plasmid strand.
evidence: This is inferred from the smear pattern observed in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: A daily dose of TMZ results in 50 μM serum concentration.
source: In the clinic, a daily dose of TMZ results in 50 μM serum concentration and was shown to induce 5.2 x 104 and 7.3 x 105 O-alkyl and N-alkyl lesions per human genome, respectively (Kaina, personal communication).
evidence: This is cited from a personal communication with Kaina.

claim: A daily dose of TMZ induces 5.2 x 10^4 O-alkyl lesions per human genome.
source: In the clinic, a daily dose of TMZ results in 50 μM serum concentration and was shown to induce 5.2 x 104 and 7.3 x 105 O-alkyl and N-alkyl lesions per human genome, respectively (Kaina, personal communication).
evidence: This is cited from a personal communication with Kaina.

claim: A daily dose of TMZ induces 7.3 x 10^5 N-alkyl lesions per human genome.
source: In the clinic, a daily dose of TMZ results in 50 μM serum concentration and was shown to induce 5.2 x 104 and 7.3 x 105 O-alkyl and N-alkyl lesions per human genome, respectively (Kaina, personal communication).
evidence: This is cited from a personal communication with Kaina.

claim: Among the 5.2 x 10^4 O6mG lesions, approximately 6240 are likely to contain an N-alkyl lesion within a 1000 nt excision track.
source: In other words, among the 5.2 x 104 O6mG lesions, ≈6240 are likely to contain an N-alkyl lesion within a 1000 nt excision track.
evidence: This is calculated based on the N-alkyl lesion density and the estimated MMR excision track size.

claim: A dose of 2 mM MNU would lead to 16,000 DSBs per genome.
source: As MNU and TMZ exhibit similar reactivities (Moody and Wheelhouse, 2014) (Kaina personal communication), a dose of 2 mM MNU would lead to 3 x 109 x 0.06/11,300 = 16,000 DSBs per genome.
evidence: This is calculated by extrapolating from the in vitro data to a human genome.

claim: The estimated amount of DSBs per genome from a 50 μM TMZ dose would be approximately 10.
source: In the clinic, the level of TMZ in the serum reaches up to 50 μM, that is 40 times less than the 2 mM dose used in vitro. Given the quadratic dose-response, the estimated amount of DSBs per genome would be 1600 times less, that is ≈10.
evidence: This is calculated by extrapolating from the in vitro data using the quadratic dose-response relationship.

claim: The conversion rate of a lesion arrangement at-risk into an actual DSB is approximately 0.16%.
source: Let's note that the conversion rate of a lesion arrangement at-risk into an actual DSB appears to be quite low (10/6240 ≈0.16%), reflecting the requirement for simultaneous occurrence of two repair events (MMR and BER).
evidence: This is calculated from the estimated number of DSBs and lesion arrangements at-risk.

claim: TMZ is presently the first-line and only anti-cancer drug in glioblastoma therapy.
source: The alkylating agent TMZ, a chemical mimic of MNU, is presently the first-line and only anti-cancer drug in glioblastoma therapy (Moody and Wheelhouse, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Moody and Wheelhouse, 2014.

claim: A daily dose of TMZ may lead to approximately 10 DSBs/cell resulting from BER/MMR crosstalk.
source: As estimated above, a daily dose of TMZ may lead to an ≈10 DSBs/cell resulting from BER/MMR crosstalk, a number comparable to the number of DSBs induced by 0.5–1 Gy of ionizing radiations (IR).
evidence: This is an extrapolation from the in vitro data to clinical doses.

claim: The number of DSBs from a daily dose of TMZ is comparable to the number of DSBs induced by 0.5-1 Gy of ionizing radiations.
source: As estimated above, a daily dose of TMZ may lead to an ≈10 DSBs/cell resulting from BER/MMR crosstalk, a number comparable to the number of DSBs induced by 0.5–1 Gy of ionizing radiations (IR).
evidence: This is a comparison based on the estimated DSB numbers.

claim: The treatment TMZ plus radiotherapy exhibits supra-additive cytotoxicity as long as TMZ administration precedes radiotherapy.
source: Moreover, it was established empirically that the treatment TMZ plus radiotherapy exhibits supra-additive cytotoxicity as long as TMZ administration precedes radiotherapy (Bobola et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Bobola et al., 2010.

claim: The ssDNA stretches formed during MMR processing at O6mG:C sites constitute preferential targets for conversion of SSBs induced by IR into DSBs.
source: Indeed, the ssDNA stretches formed at early time points during MMR processing at O6mG:C sites (step three in Figure 5) constitute preferential targets for the conversion of the numerous SSBs induced by IR into DSBs, thus providing an explanation for the observed supra-additivity in the treatment when TMZ precedes IR.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis proposed to explain the supra-additive effect.

claim: A commonly used radiotherapy session involves an IR dose of 2 Gy that predominantly induces approximately 2000 SSBs and approximately 40 DSBs/cell.
source: A commonly used radiotherapy session involves an IR dose of 2 Gy that predominantly induces ≈2000 SSBs and ≈40 DSBs/cell.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about radiotherapy effects.

claim: The majority of cells in a glioblastoma tumor are not proliferating.
source: As the majority of cells in a glioblastoma tumor are not proliferating, insights into attacking non-dividing cells might be very useful in treating this almost always fatal tumor.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about glioblastoma tumors.

claim: Purified MutSα does not bind to O6mG:C base pairs.
source: Previously, it was shown that purified MutSα does not bind to O6mG:C base pairs (Yoshioka et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Yoshioka et al., 2006.

claim: There is synergy between MutSα and MutLα (and other proteins) to achieve full MMR in extracts containing many proteins.
source: Our present experiments involve extracts containing many proteins, and there is probably synergy between MutSα and MutLα (and other proteins) to achieve full MMR (Ortega et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from Ortega et al., 2021 and represents an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Activation of MMR by a single O6mG:C lesion has been reported previously.
source: Activation of MMR by a single O6mG:C lesion has been reported previously (Duckett et al., 1999).
evidence: This is cited from Duckett et al., 1999.

claim: Upon oxidative stress produced by hydrogen peroxide treatment, RAD18 and Polη are recruited to chromatin in a MSH2-MSH6 (MutSα)-dependent manner in human cells.
source: It was previously noted that upon oxidative stress, produced by hydrogen peroxide treatment, RAD18 and Polη are recruited to chromatin in a MSH2-MSH6 (MutSα)-dependent manner in human cells (Zlatanou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Zlatanou et al., 2011.

claim: The role of MutLβ (MLH1-PMS1) remains unknown.
source: While MutSα, MutSβ, and MutLα functionally participate in MMR, the role of MutLβ (MLH1-PMS1) remains unknown (Jiricny, 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Jiricny, 2006.

claim: Long-patch BER events will be detected by the UDS assay measuring incorporation of α32P-dATP.
source: Given that the assay measures incorporation of α32P-dATP, long-patch BER events (Sattler et al., 2003) will be detected, while short-patch BER events (1 nt patch) will only be detected at 3mA but not at 7mG adducts.
evidence: This is an inference about the assay's detection capabilities based on the chemistry of BER and the assay design.

claim: Short-patch BER events (1 nt patch) will only be detected at 3mA but not at 7mG adducts in the UDS assay.
source: Given that the assay measures incorporation of α32P-dATP, long-patch BER events (Sattler et al., 2003) will be detected, while short-patch BER events (1 nt patch) will only be detected at 3mA but not at 7mG adducts.
evidence: This is an inference about the assay's detection capabilities based on the chemistry of BER and the assay design.

claim: The UDS assay is biased toward the detection of events such as MMR that involve repair patches hundreds of nucleotides long.
source: The assay is clearly biased toward the detection of events such as MMR that involve repair patches hundreds of nucleotides long.
evidence: This is an inference about the assay's detection bias based on the patch sizes of different repair pathways.

claim: Short-patch BER events are mediated by Polβ (X family), which are insensitive to aphidicolin.
source: Short-patch BER events are mediated by Polβ (X family), which are insensitive to aphidicolin.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about BER and polymerase sensitivity to aphidicolin.

claim: The modest sensitivity of MMS-induced UDS to aphidicolin is probably due to a fraction of BER events that belong to the long-patch BER pathway mediated by Polδ/ε.
source: The modest sensitivity of MMS-induced UDS to aphidicolin is probably due to a fraction of BER events that belong to the long-patch BER pathway mediated by Polδ/ε (Sattler et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an inference based on the aphidicolin sensitivity data and knowledge of BER pathways, with citation to Sattler et al., 2003.

claim: The MGMT inhibitor Patrin-2 had no effect on UDS of MNU-treated plasmid, even at a dose of 200 μM.
source: Importantly, the MGMT inhibitor Patrin-2 had no effect on UDS of MNU-treated plasmid, even at a dose of 200 μM (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Inhibition of MGMT by Patrin-2 was previously shown to occur in Xenopus extracts.
source: Surprisingly, inhibition of MGMT by Patrin-2 was previously shown to occur in Xenopus extracts (Olivera Harris et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Olivera Harris et al., 2015.

claim: Addition of aphidicolin to NPE led to more severe reduction in incorporation into MNU (approximately 3.7-fold) compared to MMS-treated plasmids (approximately 1.6-fold).
source: Addition of aphidicolin led to more severe reduction in incorporation into MNU (≈3.7-fold)- compared to MMS-treated plasmids (≈1.6-fold) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There was a greater than 70% loss in radioactivity in MNU lanes comparing -Aph versus +Aph conditions.
source: Indeed, the observed DNA degradation can specifically be linked to repair events as the loss in radioactivity in MNU lanes -Aph versus +Aph is >70% (Figure 2C; 32P image).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: HSS was shown to be proficient for MMR at a single O6mG provided a nick is present in proximity.
source: Although, HSS contains lower concentrations of most DNA repair enzymes compared to NPE, HSS was shown to be proficient for MMR at a single O6mG provided a nick is present in proximity (Olivera Harris et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Olivera Harris et al., 2015.

claim: HSS might not contain adequate concentrations of the DNA glycosylase AAG.
source: We reasoned that HSS might not contain adequate concentrations of the DNA glycosylase AAG, which initiates BER at N-alkyl sites.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the lack of repair synthesis in HSS.

claim: Loading of PCNA by RFC normally requires a single-stranded nick.
source: Loading of PCNA by RFC normally requires a single-stranded nick but it was also shown to occur, although less efficiently, on ccc DNA (Pluciennik et al., 2013; Pluciennik et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Pluciennik et al., 2013 and Pluciennik et al., 2010.

claim: PCNA loading was shown to occur, although less efficiently, on ccc DNA.
source: Loading of PCNA by RFC normally requires a single-stranded nick but it was also shown to occur, although less efficiently, on ccc DNA (Pluciennik et al., 2013; Pluciennik et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Pluciennik et al., 2013 and Pluciennik et al., 2010.

claim: Under conditions where PCNA loads on ccc DNA, PCNA loading and MMR processing lack strand directionality.
source: Under these conditions, PCNA loading and MMR processing lack strand directionality.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of PCNA loading on ccc DNA.

claim: Processing of N-alkyl adducts by BER creates repair intermediates (nicks) that stimulate PCNA loading.
source: With respect to the mechanism by which MMR activity, at a single O6mG:C lesion, becomes stimulated several folds by the presence of N-alkyl adducts, we propose that processing of N-alkyl adducts by BER creates repair intermediates (nicks) that stimulate PCNA loading.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis proposed to explain the stimulation of MMR by N-alkyl adducts.

claim: BER intermediates formed at oxidized purines or U residues can stimulate MMR processing.
source: It was previously shown that BER intermediates formed at oxidized purines or U residues can stimulate MMR processing (Repmann et al., 2015; Schanz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Repmann et al., 2015 and Schanz et al., 2009.

claim: In vitro processing of neighboring G/U mispairs by BER and ncMMR was shown to lead to DSBs.
source: Similarly, in vitro processing of neighboring G/U mispairs by BER and ncMMR was shown to lead to DSBs (Bregenhorn et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Bregenhorn et al., 2016.

claim: The extent of DNA alkylation triggered by MNU in vitro fits surprisingly well with the amount of alkylation induced by TMZ in cells at equal concentrations.
source: The extent of DNA alkylation triggered by MNU in vitro, as deduced from our alkaline cleavage determination, fits surprisingly well with the amount of alkylation induced by TMZ in cells at equal concentrations (Moody and Wheelhouse, 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison with data cited from Moody and Wheelhouse, 2014.

claim: MNU and TMZ exhibit similar reactivities.
source: As MNU and TMZ exhibit similar reactivities (Moody and Wheelhouse, 2014) (Kaina personal communication), a dose of 2 mM MNU would lead to 3 x 109 x 0.06/11,300 = 16,000 DSBs per genome.
evidence: This is cited from Moody and Wheelhouse, 2014 and a personal communication with Kaina.

claim: During cancer treatment, a dose of TMZ is delivered concomitantly with a radiotherapy session daily, for 6 weeks.
source: During cancer treatment, a dose of TMZ is delivered concomitantly with a radiotherapy session daily, for 6 weeks (for a recent review, see Strobel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from Strobel et al., 2019 and represents established clinical practice.

claim: The cytotoxicity of alkylating agents forming O6mG adducts was strongly influenced by the status of the MMR pathway in E. coli.
source: Work in E. coli provided elegant genetic evidence that the cytotoxicity of alkylating agents forming O6mG adducts (such as N-methyl-N'-nitrosoguanidine and MNU), including formation of replication-independent DSB, was strongly influenced by the status of the MMR pathway (Karran and Marinus, 1982; Nowosielska and Marinus, 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Karran and Marinus, 1982 and Nowosielska and Marinus, 2008.

claim: Formation of replication-independent DSB by alkylating agents forming O6mG adducts was strongly influenced by the status of the MMR pathway in E. coli.
source: Work in E. coli provided elegant genetic evidence that the cytotoxicity of alkylating agents forming O6mG adducts (such as N-methyl-N'-nitrosoguanidine and MNU), including formation of replication-independent DSB, was strongly influenced by the status of the MMR pathway (Karran and Marinus, 1982; Nowosielska and Marinus, 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Karran and Marinus, 1982 and Nowosielska and Marinus, 2008.

claim: Xenopus egg-derived extracts recapitulate most forms of DNA repair.
source: We addressed this question using Xenopus egg-derived extracts, which recapitulate most forms of DNA repair (Wühr et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Wühr et al., 2014.

claim: Activation of MMR in the absence of replication in cells treated by SN1-methylating agents has been described as noncanonical MMR (ncMMR).
source: Previous studies have described activation of MMR in the absence of replication in cells treated by SN1-methylating agents, a process termed noncanonical MMR (ncMMR) (Peña-Diaz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Peña-Diaz et al., 2012.

claim: Inactivation of the AAG glycosylase suppresses DSB formation from MMS treatment.
source: Indeed, inactivation of the AAG glycosylase, the BER-initiating enzyme, suppresses DSB while inactivation of Polβ leads to their exacerbation (Simonelli et al., 2017; Tang et al., 2011; Trivedi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from Simonelli et al., 2017; Tang et al., 2011; Trivedi et al., 2005.

claim: Inactivation of Polβ leads to exacerbation of DSB formation from MMS treatment.
source: Indeed, inactivation of the AAG glycosylase, the BER-initiating enzyme, suppresses DSB while inactivation of Polβ leads to their exacerbation (Simonelli et al., 2017; Tang et al., 2011; Trivedi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from Simonelli et al., 2017; Tang et al., 2011; Trivedi et al., 2005.

claim: The toxicity of N-alkyl adducts was found to depend on cell type.
source: The toxicity of N-alkyl adducts was found to depend on cell type.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: AAG-mediated repair of N-alkyl adducts was found to mitigate toxicity in mouse ES cells and HeLa cells.
source: AAG-mediated repair of N-alkyl adducts was found to mitigate toxicity in mouse ES cells and HeLa cells, while repair was shown to cause toxic intermediates in retina and bone marrow cells (Meira et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Meira et al., 2009.

claim: AAG-mediated repair of N-alkyl adducts was shown to cause toxic intermediates in retina and bone marrow cells.
source: AAG-mediated repair of N-alkyl adducts was found to mitigate toxicity in mouse ES cells and HeLa cells, while repair was shown to cause toxic intermediates in retina and bone marrow cells (Meira et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Meira et al., 2009.

claim: O-alkyl adducts were found to be highly cytotoxic and mutagenic.
source: In all cell types, O-alkyl adducts were found to be highly cytotoxic and mutagenic.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The mutagenicity of O6mG is easily accounted for by its high propensity to mispair with T during DNA synthesis.
source: While the mutagenicity of O6mG is easily accounted for by its high propensity to mispair with T during DNA synthesis (Bhanot and Ray, 1986; Loechler et al., 1984; Mazon et al., 2010), its cytotoxicity is intriguing since O6mG per se does not interfere with DNA synthesis.
evidence: This is cited from Bhanot and Ray, 1986; Loechler et al., 1984; Mazon et al., 2010.

claim: O6mG per se does not interfere with DNA synthesis.
source: While the mutagenicity of O6mG is easily accounted for by its high propensity to mispair with T during DNA synthesis (Bhanot and Ray, 1986; Loechler et al., 1984; Mazon et al., 2010), its cytotoxicity is intriguing since O6mG per se does not interfere with DNA synthesis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Cytotoxicity of O6mG stems from a secondary lesion that forms when DNA synthesis occurs across O6mG template adducts.
source: These data led the authors to surmise that cytotoxicity stems from a secondary lesion that forms when DNA synthesis occurs across O6mG template adducts (Plant and Roberts, 1971).
evidence: This is cited from Plant and Roberts, 1971.

claim: MNU-mediated inhibition of DNA synthesis is due to the action of the MMR machinery that acts on O6mG:T lesions that form upon DNA synthesis.
source: It was demonstrated later that MNU-mediated inhibition of DNA synthesis, in the first and the second cycle, is due to the action of the MMR machinery that acts on O6mG:T lesions that form upon DNA synthesis (Goldmacher et al., 1986; Kat et al., 1993; Noonan et al., 2012; Plant and Roberts, 1971; Quiros et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Goldmacher et al., 1986; Kat et al., 1993; Noonan et al., 2012; Plant and Roberts, 1971; Quiros et al., 2010.

claim: The futile MMR cycling model has received experimental support in vitro.
source: The MMR cycling model has received experimental support in vitro (York and Modrich, 2006) and in Escherichia coli (Mazon et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from York and Modrich, 2006.

claim: The futile MMR cycling model has received experimental support in Escherichia coli.
source: The MMR cycling model has received experimental support in vitro (York and Modrich, 2006) and in Escherichia coli (Mazon et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Mazon et al., 2010.

claim: Studies with synchronized cells have shown that the critical events related to cytotoxicity occur in the second cell cycle post-treatment.
source: Studies with synchronized cells have shown that the critical events related to cytotoxicity occur in the second cell cycle post-treatment (Quiros et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Quiros et al., 2010.

claim: There is more evidence that the critical cytotoxic response to methylating agents is the consequence of direct MMR processing rather than being mediated by a mere signaling model.
source: However, presently, there is more evidence that the critical cytotoxic response to methylating agents is the consequence of direct MMR processing rather than being mediated by a mere signaling model (Cejka and Jiricny, 2008; Karran, 2001; Liu et al., 2010; York and Modrich, 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Cejka and Jiricny, 2008; Karran, 2001; Liu et al., 2010; York and Modrich, 2006.
